title: Unsettlement: The Value Leaders and Artists Share
author: Jim Salvucci
summary: Salvucci uses Bob Dylan, and jazz artists like John Coltrane and Henry Threadgill, to draw out a value he calls "unsettlement": the artist's and leader's shared refusal to rest on past success. Dylan, still touring and reinventing his songs at 85, treats even his own sacred texts as unfinished, frustrating fans who want faithful reproductions but giving audiences what they need. Through Dylan's fearless one-off Letterman performance, his fallow-then-persistent 1980s, and jazz's ethos that no performance is ever final, Salvucci argues leaders should be self-aware but not self-satisfied, disciplined in a way true to themselves, and willing to smash their own conventions and build anew. The shared value is an audacious commitment to unsettlement.
points: "Unsettlement" is the value leaders and artists share: a restless refusal to rest on past success, always searching not just for something different but something better.
Dylan, touring and reworking his songs at 85, gives audiences what they need rather than faithful reproductions of the golden oldies they want.
His fearless, high-stakes moves, the one-off punk "Jokerman" on Letterman, a failed Live Aid, model a leader unafraid to fail in front of huge audiences.
Jazz masters like Coltrane and Threadgill must secure true mastery before they can "let loose"; boundary-breaking rests on discipline and self-awareness.
Leaders should be self-aware but not self-satisfied, disciplined in a way true to themselves, and willing to challenge assumptions and smash their own conventions to reach another level.
quotes: Dylan, even today at age 85, is restless as an artist—always searching for something else, not just different but better.
That performing even old standards is a creative act, each time, every time—a challenge to the audience. That no performance is ever final or definitive.
He converted restlessness into persistence until he found his depth again. He leaned toward the artist’s and leader’s shared value I call unsettlement.

Be self-aware but not self-satisfied. Be disciplined in a way that’s true to yourself. Build wisely. And be willing to take risks, challenge assumptions, smash conventions—even your own—and build anew to get to another level.
Great leaders enact artistic sensibility by building—and breaking—with bold sincerity, unrelenting integrity, and fearlessness.
Like great artists, great leaders don’t give up, don’t sit back, don’t sit it out. That’s the value that leaders and artists share most—an audacious commitment to unsettlement.
